posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the 'explainability' gap as the real blocker, not AI itself, and plant the seed that the problem is attribution not intelligence
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense — the problem was never the AI, it was that nobody could trace the answer back to anything auditable. 'GPT said so' isn't a methodology, it's a shrug. The analysts I talk to aren't asking for less AI, they're asking for outputs they can actually stand behind when someone puts them in a room with a regulator. How many tools are even designed with that accountability layer in mind?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the trust gap insight, add a sharper layer on why it happens, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The trust problem is almost always the same thing underneath — the finance team can't see how the numbers were built, so they don't believe them. Excel feels safer because they made it themselves. 18 months of build doesn't fix that, and honestly neither does a better dashboard. What would it have taken for them to trust it enough to own it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why dashboards get bloated in the first place' layer
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs usually means 47 different people who got to add their metric and nobody who had to defend why it mattered. The cut from 10% to 85% usage is the real number here — that's not a dashboard improvement, that's the difference between a reporting exercise and something people actually trust. I keep seeing teams treat more coverage as more value, when usually it's just more noise with a nicer colour scheme. What made the hardest conversation — deciding which 5, or getting buy-in to kill the other 42?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post that nails the self-service BI failure mode — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the missing layer about definitions not tools
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem isn't a Power BI problem, it's a 'nobody agreed on the definitions before the licenses got handed out' problem. The tool just makes the disagreement visible faster. Most teams I talk to think they need better dashboards when what they actually need is one person with the authority to say 'this is what revenue means, full stop.' Who's playing that role at most orgs right now?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk (not just accuracy) with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing shift here is the important bit — treating AI outputs as untrusted inputs rather than trusted answers. Most analytics tools are still designed to look authoritative by default, which is exactly the wrong default when the numbers might be wrong. Someone has to make the call on what gets cited in a board deck or a compliance report, and right now that accountability is just... floating. Who in your org currently owns that sign-off?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the £200k waste pattern, add the real reason it happens, leave them thinking
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is painfully common — and the real problem usually isn't the tool, it's that 'self-service' got sold to the CFO but never actually designed for the operations lead or the account manager who needed it. Most platforms assume the person asking the question can also write the query. Those aren't the same person. Who even signed off on the purchase — IT or the business team who were supposed to use it?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm naming a real governance pain point — validate the culture diagnosis, add the nuance that tooling often makes the culture problem invisible until it's too late
posts.draft_comment: The 'three teams, three filter sets' thing is so common it's almost a rite of passage. And you're right that AI doesn't fix it — if anything it just makes the disagreement faster. The part I'd push back on slightly: sometimes the tooling is quietly encouraging the behaviour, making it too easy for each team to define their own version of 'correct'. What does the CFO do with the numbers now — wait for someone to adjudicate, or just pick the one they trust most?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director exposing the adoption gap in enterprise AI rollouts — validate the shadow AI observation and reframe the real problem as prompting literacy, not tool quality
posts.draft_comment: The shadow AI thing is the honest part of this post. When people sneak off to ChatGPT on their phones it's not defiance — it's just that the friction-to-value ratio is way off. The 'nobody knows what to ask it' problem is real and I don't think more training solves it. What does the 12% who actually use it have in common?
